text: Vegetation appears before the Sun in verse 16. The scientific formation model has the Sun forming before Earth and therefore before terrestrial plants.
scope: Comparison assumes the days give a literal physical sequence; a literary reading makes a different claim.
summary: On a literal timeline, plants appear before the Sun. Science places the Sun before Earth and its plants.

text: The Sun helps mark days and years; the yearly seasonal cycle relates to Earth’s tilted axis and orbit.
scope: Agreement with observable cycles does not establish the chapter’s creation sequence.
summary: The Sun helps mark days and years. Earth’s tilt and orbit explain the seasonal cycle.

text: This places the Sun after Earth and vegetation. NASA’s formation model has the Sun forming first from the solar nebula, with the remaining material forming planets.
scope: Disagreement concerns a literal chronological reading, not the metaphor of heavenly lights.
summary: On a literal timeline, the Sun appears after Earth and plants. Science places the Sun first.

text: The day–night pattern broadly agrees with Earth rotating so different regions face toward or away from the Sun.
scope: This is agreement with the observed pattern, not evidence that every detail of the account is scientific.
summary: The day–night pattern agrees with Earth rotating toward and away from the Sun.

text: If “not be removed” means Earth is physically motionless, that conflicts with Earth’s rotation and orbit around the Sun.
scope: The passage is poetry. Stability or permanence is another reading; the disagreement applies to physical immobility.
summary: If this poem means Earth never moves, it conflicts with Earth’s rotation and orbit. Stability is another possible meaning.

text: River water reaches the sea and circulates through the water cycle by evaporation, precipitation, and runoff.
scope: Broad observational agreement; the verse does not provide a complete hydrological explanation.
summary: Rivers flowing to the sea broadly fit the water cycle, though the verse does not explain the full process.

text: The image of water rising and returning as rain broadly aligns with evaporation, condensation, and precipitation.
scope: A poetic description, not a complete scientific model.
summary: The poetic description of water rising and returning as rain broadly fits the water cycle.

text: The image of water rising and returning as rain broadly aligns with evaporation, condensation, and precipitation.
scope: A poetic description, not a complete scientific model.
summary: The poetic description of water rising and returning as rain broadly fits the water cycle.

text: Josephus describes Herod as a historical ruler of Judea.
scope: Corroborates the ruler and setting; does not independently establish Jesus’s birth or the visit of the magi.
summary: Josephus confirms Herod ruled Judea. This supports the setting, not the birth story itself.

text: Josephus describes Archelaus succeeding Herod and receiving authority over Judea.
scope: Supports the succession. Archelaus’s formal Roman title was ethnarch; it does not independently verify the family’s journey.
summary: Josephus confirms Archelaus succeeded Herod in Judea. This supports the succession, not the family’s journey.

text: Josephus places the census under Quirinius after Archelaus’s removal, which came after Herod’s death. This conflicts with placing that same census in the Herod-era birth setting.
scope: A chronological tension assuming this is the census Josephus describes. Other proposed readings require additional evidence.
summary: Josephus places Quirinius’s census after Herod’s death. Using that census for a Herod-era birth creates a chronological conflict.

text: Josephus records Pilate governing Judea under Tiberius.
scope: Supports those officials and their setting; does not verify every date, title, or named ruler in this verse.
summary: Josephus records Pilate governing Judea under Tiberius. This supports those officials and the setting.

text: Josephus also describes Judas the Galilean’s opposition to the census under Quirinius.
scope: Supports the existence of a census-related movement, not every detail of its leader’s death or followers’ dispersal.
summary: Josephus also describes Judas the Galilean opposing Quirinius’s census. This supports the movement, not every detail of the verse.
